segments.text: The House and Senate are deliberately different institutions, not two versions of the same chamber — lawmaking requires negotiation across two bodies with genuinely different rules, terms and powers.

items.text: Congress’s constitutional authority over taxation and appropriations, among its strongest checks on the executive.
Make a House-versus-Senate table; learn the bill process from introduction through committees, both chambers, conference and presidential action; add each chamber’s special constitutional powers.
Do not say House and Senate have identical powers.
Do not treat committees as minor administrative units; they are central to lawmaking and oversight.
Do not assume the president can spend federal money without congressional appropriations.
The House is apportioned by population with two-year terms; the Senate gives two senators per state with six-year staggered terms.
The House has sole power of impeachment; the Senate conducts impeachment trials and confirms treaties/nominations.
Congress controls federal appropriations and taxation.
Know precisely what both chambers share, what only one chamber can do, and how Congress checks the executive through law, money and oversight.
Foreign policy is constitutionally shared between Congress and the president — never solely presidential, despite common popular assumption.
